QF.id: SIA Assessment Frameworks Techniques and Standards_6

question.text: An SROI ratio of 0.85:1 computed by Mr. Arjun Desai (SIA) on a livelihood program indicates:

answer.text: The SIA cannot issue an opinion because SROI ratios below 1 are inadmissible under SAS-100
For every INR 1 of social value, INR 0.85 of investment was made — the program is highly efficient
The deadweight is 85% — the assumption set must be rejected
For every INR 1 invested, INR 0.85 of social value was created — i.e., the program destroyed net social value relative to investment and is not positive

explanation.text: The Logic: SROI is the ratio of monetised Net Impact Value to the Investment that produced it, expressed as a "Net Impact Value : Investment" ratio. A ratio of 0.85:1 therefore means that every INR 1 of investment generated only INR 0.85 of monetised social value, i.e., net social value is below the cost of the intervention. A ratio of 1:1 is the conventional break-even threshold for positive social return; anything below 1:1 indicates that, on the assumptions used, the programme did not generate as much social value as the resources committed. The Trap: Option 2 inverts the ratio (it reads "for every INR 1 of social value, INR 0.85 of investment was made" - that would be Investment / Impact Value, not SROI). Option 3 conflates SROI with the deadweight percentage. Option 4 incorrectly asserts that an SROI below 1 makes the engagement inadmissible - in practice, sub-1 ratios are still reported with appropriate narrative on assumptions, sensitivities, and time-horizon effects. Note: The cited workbook pages (151, 158, 161 of the Social Impact Assessors Certification Examination Workbook) refer to SROI as a monetisation method and to comparing monetary returns against investment, but they do not, in the pages checked, define how to interpret a specific 0.85:1 ratio or state the "below-1 means net value destroyed" conclusion. The framing above reflects general SROI methodology as practised in social-impact evaluation.
